title: A living carousel from brief to beat
description: How to go from an idea to 6 animated slides with a single soundtrack: brief, half-second storyboard and synced sound. With the Clint carousel opened up, slide by slide.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that appear in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: When I started this carousel, I had three separate things in my head: the brief, the animation and the music. In my first conversation with the AI I realized that was a mistake. If the music comes later, the animation never lands right on it. Yep. I put everything into a single document, and that's the path I show here. Shall we?
1. The brief in one sentence

Before any color, I wrote the carousel's story in one line: a lead messages on WhatsApp, the AI replies right away, the conversation becomes an opportunity, the meeting gets booked, Aura shows what is stuck and the carousel ends on the free trial. Six slides, one for each step.

Then came the decisions that change the result: who it's for (people who sell through WhatsApp), the brand line ("Você pensa. A Clint faz."), the CTA (7-day free trial, confirmed on the website) and what I can't claim. A number without a source, for example, doesn't go in. That's why the conversations and data in the carousel carry an illustrative label.

And a character who runs through everything. In our case, Beto, a fictional lead. He shows up in slide 1 waiting for a reply, in 2 talking to Aura, in 3 becoming a card in the CRM and in 4 booking the meeting. Without a character, each slide becomes a disconnected ad.
How Beto and the slides got Clint's look:
2. The music sets the clock

I chose 120 beats per minute. That gives one beat every half second and one bar every 2 seconds. That's why the slides are 6 or 8 seconds long: exactly 3 or 4 bars. If a slide were 7 seconds, the loop seam would land in the middle of a bar and the ear notices.
There is just one track, in F major, with four chords that repeat. Each slide plays the next section of the same song. Whoever swipes from one slide to the next feels the music keep going.
3. The storyboard by half second

Here is the heart of the method. Each slide became a table with one row per beat: the time, what happens on screen, where the cursor is and which sound plays. The whole carousel came to 88 rows. It sounds like a lot, but each row is a decision the AI doesn't have to make up.
I used only four sounds: a pop for something appearing, a click for interaction, a whoosh for big movement and a strong hit for the slide's main moment. Pick a slide and see its score.
Look at slide 2: the strong hit lands at 4.5 seconds, exactly when "Lead qualified in 38 seconds" appears. That's the moment I want to stick. One strong moment per slide, no more.
4. The loop rule

Each slide has to end exactly the way it started. So from beat 6.0 on, everything goes back to its place. And no sound plays in the last 0.8 seconds, so there's no click at the seam. The track is generated in a circular way: the tail of each sound wraps back to the start of the file. In the video, the difference between the last frame and the first ended up below 1 on a 0 to 255 scale. The eye can't see it.
5. Sound runs on the same clock

The track was also written in code, from the same list of times as the storyboard. That guarantees the pop in the sound and the pop on screen happen on the same frame. At the end, the volume is set to -14 LUFS, the standard social networks use so they don't turn the audio down or blow it out.

Something I learned the hard way: when I redesigned slide 1, the messages changed timing and the sound stayed on the old timing. It felt off, even though nobody could say why. I updated the sound list and regenerated the track. Storyboard, screen and sound always have to move together.

blocks.caption: Turn the sound on for each slide and notice the hits. Conversations and data are illustrative.

blocks.text: If you're going to make yours, start on paper: the sentence, the character, the beat-by-beat table. The animation gets easy once the storyboard is ready. In the next tutorial I get into the detail that most changes how motion feels: the curve.
